title: Liszt’s rhapsody leaves the keyboard
work: Hungarian Rhapsody No. 2, S. 244/2 — shared opening
question: What happens to Liszt’s pauses and flourishes when one pianist becomes a whole orchestra?
intro: Liszt opens with a summons: accented chords, pauses and quick little flourishes. Rachmaninoff plays the piano original, while Stokowski’s Philadelphia players use Karl Müller-Berghaus’s orchestration. Goehr adds a London performance from Kingsway Hall; all three meet in the opening of their first disc sides.

recordings.label: Sergei Rachmaninoff, 1919
recordings.note: Rachmaninoff plays Liszt’s solo original for Edison, in his first year of gramophone recording.

recordings.label: Leopold Stokowski, Philadelphia Orchestra, 1936
recordings.note: Philadelphia plays Karl Müller-Berghaus’s orchestration, spreading Liszt’s piano writing across an orchestra.

recordings.label: Walter Goehr, National Symphony Orchestra of London, 1945
recordings.note: Goehr recorded the National Symphony Orchestra of London at Kingsway Hall in 1945.

passages.label: The opening call
passages.note: Accented chords punctuate a winding line; short flourishes dart between the broad notes.

passages.label: The slow dance
passages.note: The slow melody unfolds above a repeated bass figure, with little turns tucked between its longer notes.

passages.label: Chords beneath the melody
passages.note: The melody grows fuller in chords, while the bass keeps its heavy tread.
